## AI for Internal Audit in Indian Companies: A Practical Starting Point

URL: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-08-ai-for-internal-audit-in-indian-companies-a-practical-starting-point
Last updated: 2026-10-08
Summary: A CA's starting point for AI in internal audit in India: who s.138 covers, what ICAI's new SIA 240 on tools asks for, and one full-population test.

CA insights · 2026-10-08 · 11 min read

### AI for Internal Audit in Indian Companies: A Practical Starting Point

A CA's starting point for AI in internal audit in India: who s.138 covers, what ICAI's new SIA 240 on tools asks for, and one full-population test.

Key takeaways

- Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, under section 138, requires an internal auditor in listed companies and in unlisted public and private companies above set turnover or borrowing thresholds.
- ICAI's SIA 240 expects tools, including AI, to be validated and documented, and says the internal auditor should not rely solely on automated outputs.
- Start with full-population testing of one high-volume process, such as procure-to-pay, instead of a sample.
- AI helps turn policy into tests, draft code, group exceptions and draft observations; people decide what is an issue and sign the report.
- Under CARO 2020 clause 3(xiv), the statutory auditor reports on whether the internal audit system is commensurate with the business.

If you run internal audit in an Indian company, or your CA firm is the appointed internal auditor under section 138, here is my short answer on AI: do not start with a dashboard. Start by testing one high-volume process on the full population instead of a sample, let people investigate every exception the test throws up, and document the tool the way you would document any other audit procedure. ICAI has now written that expectation down in a standard of its own, which makes this a good year to begin properly.

I trained as a Chartered Accountant, spent my early years in Big 4 assurance, and now help finance and audit teams put AI into real workflows. The pattern I see in internal audit is the same one I saw in statutory audit: the technology is rarely the constraint. Clean data, a clear test and a reviewer who knows the business are.

### Who this applies to: section 138 and Rule 13

Internal audit is not optional for a large part of corporate India. Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 , made under section 138 of the Companies Act, 2013, requires an internal auditor in:

- every listed company;
- every unlisted public company with paid-up share capital of ₹50 crore or more, turnover of ₹200 crore or more, outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions above ₹100 crore, or outstanding deposits of ₹25 crore or more, at any point in the preceding financial year;
- every private company with turnover of ₹200 crore or more, or outstanding loans or borrowings from banks or public financial institutions above ₹100 crore, at any point in the preceding financial year.

Two details in the rule matter for AI. First, the internal auditor can be a Chartered Accountant, whether or not in practice, or an employee of the company, so the function may sit with an in-house team or an outside firm. Second, the Audit Committee or the Board, in consultation with the internal auditor, formulates the scope, functioning, periodicity and methodology of the internal audit. Moving from sampling to full-population analytics is a change of methodology. Take it to the Audit Committee before you rely on it, not after.

### What the standards now say about tools and AI

ICAI's Internal Audit Standards Board issued a revised compendium of Standards on Internal Audit in 2026 . It rationalises the earlier standards into 20 SIAs and adds new ones, including SIA 240, Use of Tools . SIA 240 names data analytics platforms, CAATs, visualisation tools, audit management software and "emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML)". It is recommendatory and effective from 1 April 2026 until the ICAI Council notifies the date from which it applies to internal audits.

The requirements read like a sensible AI policy. Paraphrasing paragraph 4:

- Plan it. Evaluate and record the proposed use of tools at the planning stage, aligned to the risk assessment.
- Validate it. Check tools for relevance, reliability, security and confidentiality, and confirm that outputs are complete and accurate. The application material suggests trial runs, benchmarking against known outcomes and cross-checks with manual procedures.
- Protect the data. Tools must comply with data privacy and cybersecurity rules, and third-party tools need confidentiality, ownership and access controls. The standard names the DPDP Act, 2023.
- Document it. Record the rationale, configuration, test parameters and outcomes, and disclose any limitation that affects the conclusion.
- Keep judgement. "The internal auditor should not rely solely on automated outputs."

The same compendium carries SIA 230 on internal audit evidence and SIA 250 on documentation, so an AI-assisted test is held to the same evidence and file standard as a manual one. Internationally, the IIA Global Internal Audit Standards , with 15 principles across five domains, took effect on 9 January 2025 , and Standard 10.3 deals with the technological resources a function needs. If your team follows both frameworks, the direction is the same.

### Where internal audit actually is with AI

It is earlier than the conference talks suggest. The IIA's 2025 North American Pulse of Internal Audit found that the share of chief audit executives using generative AI rose from 15% in the previous edition to 40%. In the same survey, 92% named data analytics as the most important technology skill for internal audit, yet only 28% described their own analytics use as high or advanced. The IIA's Vision 2035 research reported that 18% of respondents were using AI in internal audit and a further 22% were researching it.

Those surveys lean heavily towards North America, and I have not seen a comparable Indian dataset, so treat them as direction rather than benchmark. But the gap they show matches what I see: teams want generative AI, and many have not yet built the analytics habits that make it useful. Finance more broadly is similar. Gartner's 2025 AI in Finance survey found 59% of finance functions using AI, with error and anomaly detection among the three most common use cases.

### Start with full-population testing of one process

Sampling exists because testing everything used to be expensive. It is not any more. If a process produces structured data, a script can test every transaction, and the conversation with the audit committee changes from "we found nothing in 25 samples" to "we tested all of them, and here are the exceptions we investigated."

Good first candidates are processes with volume, clear rules and data you can extract from the ERP:

- Procure-to-pay: duplicate invoices, vendor master changes close to payment runs, purchase orders split to stay under an approval limit, payments to vendors who share bank details or addresses with employees.
- Employee expenses: claims on non-working days, repeated round amounts, the same receipt claimed twice, claims approved by the claimant's own reportee.
- Payroll: employees sharing bank accounts, pay to people after their exit date, changes to pay made outside the approval workflow.
- Revenue and receivables: credit notes raised shortly after period end, manual adjustments to customer balances, discounts outside the policy grid.

Pick one. The temptation to build a "continuous auditing platform" in the first quarter is strong and, in my experience, the reason many analytics programmes stall.

### Where AI helps, and where it must not decide

Most full-population testing is plain analytics: joins, filters and rules. AI earns its place around that core, and SIA 240's examples (Python scripts and AI-based applications alongside IDEA, ACL and Power BI) fit how I would use it:

- Turning policy into tests. Give an assistant the delegation-of-authority matrix or the travel policy and ask it to propose test rules. The auditor approves every rule before it runs.
- Writing the code. AI is good at drafting the SQL or Python for a test. Someone who can read it still reviews it, and the reviewed version is what goes on file.
- Grouping exceptions. When a test returns hundreds of hits, AI can cluster them by vendor, approver or pattern so the team investigates causes rather than rows.
- Drafting observations. A first draft of the finding, the risk and the recommendation, which the auditor then rewrites in the company's language and rates.

What stays human: deciding whether an exception is a real issue, the conversation with the process owner, the risk rating, the conclusion and the report. SIA 240's application material says anomalies flagged by tools should be followed up through sampling, walkthroughs or corroborative procedures. That is the line I would draw.

### A six-step way to run the first test

- 1. Scope it with the Audit Committee. One process, one period, a stated objective, and a note that the methodology is changing to full-population testing.
- 2. Get the data and prove it is complete. Extract the transactions and agree control totals to the ledger before you test anything. A brilliant test on an incomplete extract is worthless evidence.
- 3. Write and validate the tests. Draft rules from the policy (AI can help), then run them against a period where you already know the answer, which is the "benchmarking against known outcomes" SIA 240 describes.
- 4. Run on the full population. Keep the scripts, parameters and output files versioned.
- 5. Investigate exceptions. People do this. Record what was checked, what the process owner said and what evidence closed each item.
- 6. Report and document. Report what was tested and what was found, including any limits of the data, and put the tool documentation on file as SIA 240 and SIA 250 expect.

### Controls around the AI itself

Internal audit asks everyone else for controls, so its own AI use should be the best-controlled in the building. My minimum set:

- Approved tools only. Company or firm-controlled accounts with retention and training settings you have checked, never personal chatbot accounts. Payroll and vendor data contain personal data.
- Know your data-protection exposure. The DPDP Rules, 2025 were notified in November 2025 with an 18-month phased timeline, and the Act allows penalties of up to ₹250 crore for failing to maintain reasonable security safeguards. Share the minimum fields a test needs.
- A tool register. Which tools, which versions, who may use them, for what. SIA 240 suggests a centralised tool registry, version control and usage logs.
- No unreviewed output in the report. Every AI-drafted rule, script and observation has a named reviewer.

For a broader version of these review gates, see my AI controls checklist for CA firms in India .

### Remember who reads the file next

Internal audit work does not stay inside the company. Under CARO 2020 , clause 3(xiv) asks the statutory auditor whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with its size and the nature of its business, and whether the internal auditors' reports for the period were considered. If your exceptions list came from an undocumented prompt, expect questions. If it came from a validated, versioned test with a clear trail of investigation, you have made the statutory auditor's job easier, and your own position stronger.

This is also where internal audit differs from statutory audit. For the statutory side, with SA 230 documentation, read AI for audit working papers in India . For how firms are adopting AI more generally, read how audit and accounting firms in India are using AI .

### What I would tell an Audit Committee

- We will test one process on the full population this quarter, not a sample.
- Every exception will be investigated by a person, and the file will show how each one was closed.
- The tools, scripts and AI assistance will be documented in line with SIA 240, and no client or employee data will go into unapproved tools.
- We will report what the data could and could not tell us.
- If it works, we will extend it to a second process next quarter. If it does not, we will say why.

If you want a structured way to choose that first process and run it, my 90-day AI pilot playbook applies just as well to an internal audit team. The wider picture for the profession is in the AI for Chartered Accountants in India hub . If you would rather have someone map where AI pays back across your finance and audit work, that is what the AI Opportunity Audit is for.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Is internal audit mandatory for my company in India?

Section 138 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, requires an internal auditor in every listed company; in unlisted public companies with paid-up share capital of ₹50 crore or more, turnover of ₹200 crore or more, outstanding borrowings above ₹100 crore or deposits of ₹25 crore or more; and in private companies with turnover of ₹200 crore or more or outstanding borrowings above ₹100 crore. Check the thresholds against your own preceding-year figures.

#### Do ICAI's Standards on Internal Audit allow AI?

Yes. SIA 240, Use of Tools, in ICAI's 2026 compendium names AI and machine learning alongside data analytics and CAATs. It asks the internal auditor to plan and record tool use, validate tool outputs for completeness and accuracy, protect data, document configurations and results, and not rely solely on automated outputs. It is recommendatory from 1 April 2026 until the ICAI Council notifies a mandatory date.

#### What is the best first AI use case for an internal audit team?

In my view, full-population testing of one high-volume process, such as procure-to-pay or employee expense claims. It replaces sampling with a complete test, the exceptions are easy to verify, and it fits the evidence and documentation requirements the team already follows.

#### Does the statutory auditor look at internal audit work?

Yes. Under CARO 2020, clause 3(xiv), the statutory auditor reports whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with its size and nature, and whether the internal auditors' reports were considered. AI-assisted work therefore needs to be documented well enough for another auditor to follow.

#### Will AI replace internal auditors?

No. It changes the work. Testing every transaction becomes cheap; deciding which exceptions matter, talking to process owners, rating findings and standing behind the report still need an experienced person. SIA 240 says as much: tool findings need professional scepticism and contextual evaluation.

## ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini: Which AI Assistant Suits a CA Firm?

URL: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-05-chatgpt-vs-copilot-vs-gemini-how-a-ca-firm-in-india-should-choose-an-ai-assistant
Last updated: 2026-10-05
Summary: ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot or Gemini for a CA practice in India? Compare data terms, permissions and retention, with a decision rubric for partners.

CA insights · 2026-10-05 · 7 min read

### ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini? How a CA Firm in India Should Choose an AI Assistant

Choosing between ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Gemini for a CA practice in India: where client files live, data terms, permissions, retention and a decision rubric for partners.

Key takeaways

- First decision: client work happens only in a firm-controlled business workspace, never a personal account.
- Each vendor publishes business-tier data commitments; they do not cover personal or free accounts.
- The deciding factor is where client files already live: Microsoft 365 points to Copilot, Google Workspace to Gemini.
- Clean up client-folder permissions first, because integrated assistants surface existing permission mistakes.
- Choose with a two-week bake-off on anonymised real tasks marked by one reviewer, not a demo.

A question I hear more and more from partners in Indian CA practices is no longer “should we use AI?” It is “which one should we pay for: ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini?” Usually an associate has already been using one of them on a personal account, a partner has seen a demo of another, and the IT vendor is pushing the third.

My answer is rarely about which model writes the best paragraph. For a practice that holds client financials, PAN and payroll data, unpublished results and tax positions, the deciding questions are duller: where do your client files already live, who can see what, what does the vendor contractually do with your prompts, and can you prove afterwards who used the tool on which engagement? Get those right and any of the three can be a sensible choice. Get them wrong and the best model in the world is a confidentiality problem with a monthly invoice.

### First, take personal accounts off the table

Every comparison below is about the business tiers. A free or personal subscription that an associate signed up for with a Gmail address is not covered by the commitments these vendors publish for organisational customers, and the firm has no admin control over it. Your confidentiality obligations to clients under ICAI’s framework do not change because a tool is convenient, and where the material includes personal data, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 expects reasonable security safeguards, including when a processor handles that data on your behalf.

So the first decision is not which vendor. It is that client work happens only inside a firm-controlled workspace, and personal accounts are for nothing that identifies a client.

### What each vendor says about your data

I would rather you read the vendors’ own pages than rely on my summary, and the links are in the Sources section. As published when I checked them on 5 October 2026:

- Microsoft 365 Copilot (which Microsoft now calls Microsoft Copilot) states that prompts, responses and data accessed through Microsoft Graph are not used to train foundation models, and that Copilot only surfaces organisational data the individual user already has at least view permission for. Admins can apply retention policies to Copilot interactions through Microsoft Purview. Microsoft also notes that customers outside the EU may have queries processed in the US, EU or other regions.
- ChatGPT business plans (Business and Enterprise): OpenAI states it does not train its models on business data by default, that you own your inputs and outputs where allowed by law, and that workspace admins control retention, with deleted conversations removed within 30 days unless legally required to be kept.
- Gemini in Google Workspace : Google’s privacy hub states that your content is not human-reviewed or used for generative AI model training outside your domain without permission, that Gemini does not access Workspace content the user lacks permission for, and that admins set how long prompts and responses are retained.

On paper, the headline promises look similar. The differences that matter to a CA practice sit underneath them.

### The real decision: where your files already live

If the firm runs on Microsoft 365, with engagement folders in SharePoint or OneDrive and client correspondence in Outlook, Copilot’s main advantage is that it works inside that permission model rather than asking people to upload files somewhere new. If the firm runs on Google Workspace, the same logic points to Gemini. ChatGPT is a standalone workspace: strong for drafting, research and analysis on documents you deliberately give it, but every file is a conscious upload, which some partners actually prefer because it forces a decision each time.

There is a catch with the integrated options that I would raise with any practice. Copilot and Gemini respect existing permissions, which means they also expose existing permission mistakes. If an articled assistant technically has view access to the entire “Clients” drive because nobody ever tightened it, an assistant that can search everything they can see will happily summarise a client file they were never meant to open. Before switching on either, run a permissions review on client folders. It is unglamorous work and it is the single most useful thing you can do first.

### A decision rubric you can use in a partners’ meeting

| Question | What good looks like | Red flag |
| Where do client files live today? | The assistant works inside the system you already govern | Staff copying files into a second, ungoverned location |
| Are folder permissions clean? | Access by engagement team, reviewed recently | “Everyone” or firm-wide access to client folders |
| Is client data used for training? | Written “no” in the business terms you sign | Only a marketing page, or a personal-tier account |
| Who controls retention? | Firm admin sets it and can apply it centrally | Each user decides, or nobody knows |
| Where is data processed? | Answered in writing by the vendor for your plan | Assumed rather than confirmed |
| Can you see who used it on what? | Admin search or export of interactions | No log beyond each user’s own history |
| Does it help with your actual work? | Fewer reviewer edits on your own test tasks | Judged only on a vendor demo |

Notice that only the last row is about output quality. The rest are about control, and for a professional practice that is the right weighting.

From pratikbajoria.com

Buy tools after you know which workflow pays back. Start with the free AI Opportunity Scorecard , or see the scoped AI Opportunity Audit for a 90-day map.

### Run a two-week bake-off, not a demo

Demos are built to impress. A bake-off is built to reveal. Pick three or four tasks your team really does, prepare anonymised or dummy versions, and run the same tasks through each shortlisted tool. Examples I would use: turning a senior’s rough notes into a clean working-paper narrative, summarising a long agreement to direct a reviewer’s attention, drafting a first reply to a routine departmental query from redacted facts, and building a checklist from a circular.

Have the same reviewer mark every output. Track how much they had to change, what they caught that was wrong, and how long the whole cycle took compared with doing it the usual way. Write it down. The tool that needs the fewest corrections on your own work is the one that earns the licence, not the one with the best launch video.

### What I would not do

I would not buy all three “to see which sticks”; that guarantees three half-adopted tools and three sets of terms to monitor. I would not let associates expense personal subscriptions and call it a pilot. I would not paste anything that identifies a client into any tool before the firm has chosen one, set retention, and written down what is allowed. And I would not let the choice of assistant substitute for review: every output that reaches a client or a file still needs a named person who checked it.

Whichever you choose, the controls that make it safe are the same, and I have set them out in the AI controls checklist for CA firms in India . For the full implementation map, start at the AI for chartered accountants in India hub. If GST is your first use case, read using AI for GST reconciliation without risking client data ; for assurance work, see AI for audit working papers in India . To see where AI pays back across your practice, take the free AI Opportunity Scorecard , look at the scoped AI Opportunity Audit , or book a discovery call .

### Monday-morning checklist

- Write one line in the firm’s policy: no client-identifying data in personal AI accounts.
- List where client files actually live: Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, local drives or practice software.
- Review permissions on client folders before enabling Copilot or Gemini.
- Read each shortlisted vendor’s business data terms and save a dated copy.
- Ask each vendor in writing where your prompts are processed and stored.
- Prepare three or four anonymised test tasks and name one reviewer to mark them.
- Decide who in the firm administers retention and can search usage.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Is ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini safest for client data in a CA firm?

None is safe or unsafe on its own. Each vendor publishes data commitments for its business tiers, and those commitments do not cover personal accounts. Safety depends on using a firm-controlled business workspace, clean folder permissions, admin-set retention and a review step before anything reaches a client.

#### Should a firm on Microsoft 365 automatically choose Copilot?

It is usually the natural starting point because it works inside the permission model you already manage. But clean up client-folder permissions first, and still run a short bake-off on your own tasks before committing licences across the firm.

#### Can associates keep using their personal ChatGPT accounts for non-client work?

That is a firm policy decision. The practical rule I suggest is simple: personal accounts may be used for general learning, never for anything that identifies a client, an engagement or a person.

## AI Courses for Chartered Accountants in India: What Is Worth It

URL: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-ai-courses-for-chartered-accountants-in-india-what-is-worth-it
Last updated: 2026-10-07
Summary: AI courses for chartered accountants in India in 2026: what ICAI’s AICA Levels 1–3 cost and cover, when a paid course helps, and how to learn on real work.

CA insights · 2026-10-07 · 7 min read

### AI Courses for Chartered Accountants in India: What Is Actually Worth It

Best AI courses for chartered accountants in India in 2026: what ICAI’s AICA Levels 1–3 cost and cover, when a paid course helps, and how to learn AI on your own client work.

Key takeaways

- Start with ICAI's AICA Level 1: three days for ₹5,000 plus GST, with 18 structured CPE hours.
- AICA Level 2 costs ₹10,000 plus GST; Level 3 was launched in June 2026.
- CA GPT is free for ICAI members and a zero-cost place to start.
- Before paying for a private course, check it uses Indian CA work, has you build something and teaches review and data rules.
- A course will not fix implementation: pick one workflow, take a baseline and write a one-page data rule.

If you are a chartered accountant in India looking for an AI course, start with ICAI’s own AI for Chartered Accountants (AICA) certificate, because it is cheap, earns structured CPE hours and is designed around CA work. Then spend far more time applying AI to one real workflow in your practice than collecting further certificates. A course teaches you what the tools can do; only your own files teach you where they break.

I get asked about courses every week, usually by partners who have just watched a junior do in ten minutes what used to take an afternoon. Here is how I would think about it.

### ICAI’s AICA courses: what they cost and cover

ICAI’s AI Committee runs a three-level certificate. The figures below are taken from ICAI’s own pages as I write this; check them before you book, because fees and formats change.

| Level | Format | Fee | CPE |
| AICA Level 1 | 3 days, classroom, at ICAI branches ( course guidelines ) | ₹5,000 + GST ( ICAI AI site ) | 18 structured hours |
| AICA Level 2 | 2 days online plus 3 days in person ( ICAI batch listings ) | ₹10,000 + GST ( ICAI AI site ) | See the batch details |
| AICA Level 3 | Advanced; only for members who have completed Level 2 ( launched June 2026 ) | See ICAI announcements | See ICAI announcements |

Level 1 asks for basic computer and Office skills, your own laptop and a daily online assessment, and it includes a group project on real finance and audit use cases. Scale is not a problem: ICAI reported that more than 7,500 members had registered within months of launch , and by June 2026 it said it had trained over 50,000 members in AI .

ICAI also makes CA GPT available free to members; it launched on 1 July 2024 and ICAI reported more than 70,000 members using it by November that year. If you have never tried a domain-specific assistant, that is a zero-cost place to start.

### When a paid private course is worth it

There are plenty of paid “AI for CA” programmes. Some are good. Before you pay, ask four questions:

- Does it use Indian CA work? GST reconciliation, tax audit reports, Tally exports, CARO, notices. Generic “AI for business” content will not transfer.
- Do you build something? A working prompt library, a reconciliation workflow or a checklist you can use on Monday is worth more than hours of slides.
- Does it teach review and data rules? If confidentiality, client data and checking output are not on the syllabus, the course is teaching you to create risk faster.
- Who teaches it? Someone who has implemented AI inside a practice or finance team, not only someone who demos tools.

Note that I am not naming or ranking private providers, because I have not audited their syllabuses and I will not recommend something I have not checked.

### What a course will not give you

Every partner I work with who finished a course hit the same wall: back in the office, nobody decided which workflow to change, who reviews output or what data may go into which tool. That is an implementation problem, not a skills gap. The fix is unglamorous: pick one workflow, take a baseline, write a one-page data rule and run it for ninety days with full review. My 90-day AI pilot playbook for CA firms sets out each step.

### A self-study plan that costs almost nothing

- Week 1: try CA GPT and one business-grade general assistant on a redacted sample of real work. Compare the output with what your team would have produced. My comparison of ChatGPT vs Copilot vs Gemini for a CA firm helps you choose.
- Week 2: read the AI controls checklist for CA firms and agree, in writing, what may never go into a tool.
- Weeks 3–4: apply AI to one workflow, for example AI for GST reconciliation , and log the time taken and errors caught.
- Then: take AICA Level 1 with real questions in hand. You will get far more out of three days in a classroom once you know where you are stuck.

### My recommendation

For most CAs: AICA Level 1, CA GPT and one disciplined pilot. For partners who want the whole firm moving, training alone rarely does it; you need someone to map workflows and set the controls. That is what the AI Opportunity Audit is for. For the wider picture, start at the AI for chartered accountants in India hub , see my notes on AI tools for chartered accountants , or book a discovery call .

### Frequently asked questions

#### What is the best AI course for chartered accountants in India?

For most CAs, ICAI’s AI for Chartered Accountants (AICA) Level 1 is the sensible first step: three days in a classroom for ₹5,000 plus GST, with 18 structured CPE hours, built around finance and audit use cases. Level 2 (₹10,000 plus GST, with online and in-person days) and the newer Level 3 go deeper. Check ICAI’s AI site for current fees and batches.

#### Is an AI certification useful for a CA?

A certificate shows intent, but clients and employers care about what you can do. The value comes from applying AI to a real workflow, with written data rules and review, and being able to show the time saved and errors caught.

#### How can chartered accountants learn AI for free?

Start with ICAI’s CA GPT, which is free for members, and a business-grade general assistant on redacted samples of your own work. Then apply it to one workflow for a few weeks and log what changes before paying for further training.

#### How can Chartered Accountants use AI?

Use it first on frequent, checkable work: bank categorisation, GST and TDS reconciliation exception lists, notice summaries and first drafts of client emails. Keep a named reviewer, a firm-controlled account and a written rule on which client data may be used.

## Is CA Worth It in 2026 With AI? A Chartered Accountant’s View

URL: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/2026-10-07-is-ca-worth-it-in-2026-with-ai
Last updated: 2026-10-07
Summary: Is CA worth it in 2026 now AI handles routine accounting? A practising CA weighs pass rates, membership growth and AI’s impact, and the skills that pay off.

CA insights · 2026-10-07 · 7 min read

### Is CA Worth It in 2026 With AI? A Chartered Accountant’s View

Is CA worth it in 2026 now that AI can do routine accounting? A practising CA weighs pass rates, membership growth and AI’s impact, and explains which skills make the qualification pay off.

Key takeaways

- Yes, if you treat CA as a qualification in judgement, accountability and the right to sign; it is a weak bet if you want routine accounting work.
- The exam is still hard: 14.07% of candidates who sat both groups passed CA Final in May 2026 (3,345 of 23,776).
- ICAI membership was 4,23,105 on 1 April 2025; most members work in industry, finance and other roles rather than practice.
- Skills that make CA pay off alongside AI: review and scepticism, data fluency, clear writing, controls thinking and domain depth.

Yes, CA is still worth it in 2026, but for a different reason than it was ten years ago. The qualification is no longer valuable because you can do the accounting; AI can increasingly do much of that. It is valuable because a chartered accountant is a regulated person who can sign, take responsibility and explain what the numbers mean. If you go in expecting to be paid for routine work, you will be disappointed. If you go in to become the person who reviews, judges and advises, the case is strong.

I am a CA, ex-Big 4, a founder, and I now help firms implement AI. Students and parents ask me this more than any other question, so here is my honest answer with the numbers.

### The hard part has not changed: it is a difficult exam

In ICAI’s CA Final May 2026 result , 14.07% of candidates who sat both groups passed (3,345 out of 23,776). The Group I pass rate was 12% and Group II was 20.49%. That difficulty is exactly why the qualification still carries weight. It is also why you should go in with a realistic plan for several attempts and articleship years, not a fixed timeline.

### The profession is growing, but practice is not the only path

ICAI’s 76th Annual Report put membership at 4,23,105 on 1 April 2025, up from 4,03,617 a year earlier. About 1.61 lakh members were in full-time or part-time practice; the majority work in industry, finance, consulting and other roles. So “doing CA” today often means a finance career in a company, a GCC or a start-up rather than running a practice. Those are also the roles where AI is changing the daily work fastest.

### What AI changes for a CA career

The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 expects accounting, bookkeeping and payroll clerks to be among the fastest-declining roles to 2030, with AI and information processing as primary drivers. In India, Microsoft and LinkedIn’s 2024 Work Trend Index found 92% of knowledge workers already use AI at work. Put simply: the clerical layer of accounting is shrinking, and the people who remain are expected to use AI as a matter of course.

For a CA, that means:

- Articleship will feel different. Less vouching and typing, more checking machine output and dealing with exceptions. Firms will want article assistants who can review, not just prepare.
- Entry-level value moves up. A newly qualified CA who can only do what a tool does will struggle on salary. One who can explain a variance to a CFO or defend a position in front of a department will not.
- The signature becomes more valuable, not less. Somebody has to be accountable for AI-assisted numbers. Regulators and clients want that to be a qualified person.

The institute itself is adapting: ICAI says it has trained over 50,000 members in AI and launched an advanced AI certification for members in June 2026. See my note on AI courses for chartered accountants in India .

### Who should do CA in 2026

It suits you if you enjoy reasoning about why a number is what it is, you are willing to put in years of exam preparation, and you want a regulated qualification that lets you sign, advise and move between practice and industry.

Think twice if you mainly want a stable job doing defined, repetitive accounting tasks. That is exactly the work AI is absorbing, and you can reach it faster through other routes.

### Skills that make CA pay off alongside AI

- Review and scepticism: catching the confident wrong answer, whether from a junior or a model.
- Data fluency: Excel done properly, a basic grasp of how data moves between Tally, GST and banks, and comfort with AI assistants. My guide to AI tools for chartered accountants is a starting point.
- Clear writing and explanation: clients pay for clarity.
- Controls thinking: knowing what data may go where, and why. The AI controls checklist for CA firms shows how a firm should think about it.
- Domain depth: GST, direct tax, audit or a sector. AI is broad; clients pay for depth.

### My answer

CA is worth it in 2026 if you treat it as a qualification in judgement and accountability, and learn AI as part of how you work. It is a poor bet if you are buying it for the routine work. If you are already qualified and want to see how AI changes the work in your firm, read will AI replace chartered accountants in India , start at the AI for chartered accountants in India hub , see the AI Opportunity Audit , or book a discovery call .

### Frequently asked questions

#### Is CA worth it in 2026?

Yes, if you want a regulated qualification built on judgement, accountability and the right to sign. The exam remains hard (14.07% of candidates who sat both groups passed CA Final in May 2026), and membership keeps growing. It is a weaker bet if you mainly want routine accounting work, which AI is absorbing.

#### Will AI take over Chartered Accountant jobs?

AI is taking over routine tasks such as data entry, reconciliations and first drafts. It is not taking over signing, opinions, advice or accountability, which stay with qualified CAs. The CAs most affected will be those whose work is mainly routine processing.

#### How many chartered accountants are there in India?

ICAI’s 76th Annual Report put total membership at 4,23,105 on 1 April 2025, up from 4,03,617 a year earlier. About 1.61 lakh members were in full-time or part-time practice; the rest work in industry, finance and other roles.

#### What skills should CA students learn for an AI future?

Review and professional scepticism, data and Excel fluency, comfort with AI assistants, clear writing, controls thinking and depth in a domain such as GST, direct tax or audit.

## AI for Chartered Accountants: Practical Use Cases and Control Gates

URL: https://pratikbajoria.com/blog/ai-for-chartered-accountants-practical-use-cases-and-controls
Last updated: 2026-10-07
Summary: A practical CA-led guide to AI for Chartered Accountants: five high-value use cases, review gates, data rules and a 90-day rollout plan for Indian CA firms.

CA insights · 2026-10-04 · Updated 7 Oct 2026 · 10 min read

### AI for Chartered Accountants: Practical Use Cases and Control Gates

AI is useful in a CA practice when it reduces preparation and review time without weakening evidence, confidentiality or professional accountability. Here is a practical way to choose the first workflow.

In practice, the question I hear from CA firms is not whether AI could help. It is how to pick the first workflow without putting a client file, a filing position or the firm's name at risk. The answer is less exciting than the demos, and much safer.

Direct answer: Chartered Accountants should start with bounded, repeatable work that has a clear source record and a named reviewer. The best first use cases are document extraction, reconciliation exception triage, research first drafts, management reporting drafts and client-intake checklists. Do not begin with unsupervised tax conclusions, auto-filing or a general chatbot with no process owner.

### Why AI for Chartered Accountants is a workflow question

“AI for Chartered Accountants” sounds like a software category. In practice, it is a workflow-design question. A CA firm already has a sequence: receive information, classify it, test it, investigate exceptions, prepare a conclusion and obtain review. AI can accelerate parts of that sequence, but it does not remove the need to know what the official record is, who approves a material conclusion and how an exception is resolved.

The practical test is simple: can the team explain what the system receives, what it produces, what evidence it keeps and when a human must intervene? If not, the firm is buying novelty rather than capacity.

Finance teams are moving quickly, so the decision is coming whether or not the firm plans for it. Gartner's June 2024 survey of 121 finance leaders found 58% of finance functions using AI, up 21 percentage points on 2023 . The most common uses were intelligent process automation (44%), anomaly and error detection (39%) and analytics (28%) . That is the same unglamorous territory as the five starting points below.

### Five high-value starting points

#### 1. Document extraction and classification

Invoices, bank statements, contracts, notices and supporting schedules often arrive in inconsistent formats. An AI-assisted workflow can classify documents, extract candidate fields and route incomplete items to a review queue. The control gate is not “the model was confident”; it is a source-linked check of the extracted value before it reaches a working paper, close pack or client communication.

Measure extraction accuracy by field, rework hours and the percentage of items sent to exception review. Keep the original document attached to the extracted record.

#### 2. Reconciliation exception triage

AI can help group unmatched transactions, suggest likely reasons and prioritise exceptions by value, age or risk. It should not silently write off differences or post adjustments. The reviewer should see the source transactions, the proposed match logic and the reason an item was escalated.

Start with one reconciliation type and a defined period. A narrow queue that becomes easier to review is more valuable than an ambitious autonomous reconciliation that nobody trusts.

#### 3. Research and first-draft analysis

Research assistants can help organise primary sources, create a first-pass issue list and surface questions for a professional to verify. Every material statement should be traceable to the source used. Generated text is a draft, not an authority and not a substitute for checking the current law, notification, circular or engagement context.

Use a source register with the date accessed, the source URL and the reviewer’s sign-off. This creates a better audit trail than pasting an unverified answer into a memo.

#### 4. Management reporting and commentary

Once the numbers are approved, AI can draft variance commentary, management questions and a concise operating summary. Keep the model away from the source ledger unless the access pattern is deliberate and controlled. The accounting system remains the system of record; the model helps explain approved data.

The useful metric is not “words generated”. Track reporting turnaround, reviewer edits, missed explanations and whether decision-makers receive the pack on time.

#### 5. Client intake and checklist tracking

Many practice bottlenecks begin before technical work: incomplete onboarding, missing documents, unclear scope or unanswered client questions. A controlled assistant can collect structured information, identify missing items and create a task for a named team member. It should be clear to the client when they are interacting with automation and how to reach a human.

Keep sensitive data collection proportionate. Do not ask a public chatbot to become the firm’s client file.

### The six control gates every CA firm should define

- Purpose: write the exact job the system is allowed to support.
- Data class: decide what may be processed, what must be redacted and what may not leave approved systems.
- Evidence: preserve source documents, prompts or instructions where relevant, output versions and reviewer notes.
- Human approval: name the person who approves material conclusions, client-facing advice or ledger-impacting actions.
- Exception handling: define where mismatches go, how they are prioritised and when the workflow stops.
- Measurement: baseline hours, cycle time, error/rework or exception rate before judging the pilot.

These gates turn a vague AI policy into an operating control. They also make procurement more disciplined: a tool must fit the workflow and its controls, not the other way around.

### What should stay human

Professional judgement, materiality decisions, client-specific advice, final tax positions, audit conclusions and approval of filings should remain with appropriately authorised professionals. AI can prepare, compare, summarise, classify and flag. It should not be allowed to create a false impression that accountability has moved to the software.

For a broader selection framework, see Best AI Tools for Chartered Accountants and Finance Professionals . For firm-level review gates, use the AI Controls Checklist for CA Firms in India .

### A 90-day rollout for a CA practice

Days 1–15 — Diagnose. Pick one workflow and interview the people who run it. Record volumes, systems, hand-offs, rework and the control points that cannot be skipped. If no one owns the workflow, fix ownership before buying software.

Days 16–30 — Design. Define the allowed input data, the output format, the reviewer, the exception queue and the success metric. Compare build, buy and wait options. A practical starting point is the AI Opportunity Scorecard .

Days 31–60 — Pilot. Run the narrowest useful release with a parallel review path. Sample outputs against source records and log every exception. Do not expand scope simply because the demo looks good.

Days 61–90 — Decide. Compare the baseline with the pilot, review control performance and document the decision to keep, redesign or stop. If the result survives review, standardise the workflow and plan the next use case. If the economics do not work, stopping is a successful control decision.

### Practical tool-selection questions

- Can the firm restrict access by team, client or matter?
- Can a reviewer see the source behind an extraction, answer or recommendation?
- Can the firm export logs and evidence if the vendor changes its model?
- What happens when the system is uncertain or the input is incomplete?
- Can the workflow integrate with the systems of record without creating a shadow ledger?
- Can the firm measure reviewer time and exception rates, not just usage?

Tool availability, pricing and data terms change. Evaluate current documentation and your firm’s own policies before adoption. A public risk reference such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework can help structure the conversation, but it is not a certification of a commercial product.

Get the data terms in writing. OpenAI says its business products, such as ChatGPT Enterprise and the API, are not used to train its models by default ; Microsoft says Microsoft 365 Copilot prompts and responses are not used to train its foundation models . Neither statement covers a staff member's personal account, which is why the approved-tool register matters more than the brand.

### FAQ

Start with bounded tasks such as classification, extraction, reconciliation triage, drafting and checklist tracking. Keep a named reviewer, source evidence, access controls and exception logging for every material workflow.

Document extraction, reconciliation exception triage, research first drafts, management reporting drafts and client-intake workflows are strong starting points when outputs can be checked against source records.

AI can reduce repetitive preparation and review work, but professional judgement, accountability, client context and approval of material conclusions remain human responsibilities.

Choose one workflow with measurable pain, map it, classify the data, define a human gate, baseline a metric and run a narrow test inside a 90-day roadmap.

### Conclusion

The CA practices that get real value from AI keep it deliberately boring: one workflow, one owner, one metric and one evidence trail. Start where the work is repetitive but the judgement boundary is clear. Use AI to cut preparation time and surface exceptions sooner, and keep professional accountability exactly where it already sits.

For a structured two-week diagnostic, see the AI Opportunity Audit . It is designed to turn process ambiguity into a ranked 90-day roadmap.
